citations.quote:
Use the lattice $\Gamma=\mathbb Z^d$, $d\ge1$, the finite spin dimension $q\ge1$, the local matrix algebras $\mathcal A_\Lambda$, and the max-coordinate metric $d_\infty$ of [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]]. For finite nonempty $Z\subset\Gamma$, write $\operatorname{diam}_\infty Z=\max_{x,y\in Z}d_\infty(x,y)$; for finite nonempty $X,Y\subset\Gamma$, write $\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,Y)=\min_{x\in X,y\in Y}d_\infty(x,y)$.

A **uniformly bounded finite-range interaction** is a family $\Phi(Z)\in\mathcal A_Z$, indexed by finite nonempty $Z\subset\Gamma$, such that $\Phi(Z)^*=\Phi(Z)$ and there are an integer $M\ge1$, a finite $R\ge0$, and $\kappa<\infty$ satisfying

$$\Phi(Z)=0\quad\text{if }|Z|>M\text{ or }\operatorname{diam}_\infty Z>R,\qquad\kappa:=\sup_{x\in\Gamma}\sum_{Z\ni x}\|\Phi(Z)\|<\infty.$$

The norm in this sum is the operator norm in the local matrix algebra $\mathcal A_Z$. If a model lists several terms with the same support, first add them in that local algebra; the resulting single operator is $\Phi(Z)$, and $\kappa$ uses its norm. Thus no multiplicity is implicit.

For a finite region $\Lambda\subset\Gamma$, define the **free-boundary finite-volume Hamiltonian** by summing only terms whose complete support lies inside $\Lambda$; terms meeting $\Lambda$ but extending outside it are omitted:

$$H_\Lambda:=\sum_{\varnothing\ne Z\subseteq\Lambda}\Phi(Z)\in\mathcal A_\Lambda.$$

It is a finite sum of self-adjoint matrices. For a fixed scale $\hbar>0$ and any finite $\Omega\supseteq\Lambda$, embed $H_\Lambda$ in $\mathcal A_\Omega$ by the canonical factor inclusion and define

$$\alpha_t^\Lambda(A):=e^{itH_\Lambda/\hbar}Ae^{-itH_\Lambda/\hbar}\qquad(A\in\mathcal A_\Omega,\ t\in\mathbb R).$$

These actions are compatible as $\Omega$ increases, because the extra tensor factors carry the identity. On $\mathcal A_\Lambda$ this is the ordinary finite matrix Heisenberg dynamics.

In physical SI bookkeeping, when $\Phi(Z)$ is interpreted as an energy, $\Phi(Z)$, $\kappa$, and $H_\Lambda$ have units J, $t$ has units s, and $\hbar$ is the adopted reduced Planck constant with units J s. The mathematics below uses only $\hbar>0$ and asserts no measured parameter value.

Let $\Phi$ be an interaction of [[def-qsm-bounded-finite-range-interaction]] with parameters $M,R,\kappa,\hbar$. Let $\mu>0$, let $\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d$ be finite, let $X\subseteq\Lambda$ be finite and nonempty, and let $Y\subset\mathbb Z^d$ be any finite nonempty set. Take $A\in\mathcal A_X$ and $B\in\mathcal A_Y$, with both embedded in the common finite algebra $\mathcal A_{\Lambda\cup Y}$. Then for every $t\in\mathbb R$,

$$\bigl\|[\alpha_t^\Lambda(A),B]\bigr\|\le 2\|A\|\,\|B\|\,|X|\exp\!\left(\frac{2\kappa M e^{\mu R}}{\hbar}|t|-\mu\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,Y)\right).$$

Here the finite-volume dynamics is extended by the identity on sites outside $\Lambda$, as in [[def-qsm-bounded-finite-range-interaction]]. The parameter $\mu$ is measured per lattice step in the dimensionless max-coordinate metric. The bound is uniform over finite volumes containing $X$; it is an operator-norm estimate for the stipulated spin model, not a relativistic light cone.

Fix an integer dimension $d\ge1$, the countable site set $\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}^d$ of [[lem-qsm-integer-lattice-countable]], and one finite spin dimension $q\ge1$, where $q$ is a positive integer (so $q\in\mathbb N$ and $1\le q$, by [[def-natural-numbers]] and [[def-nat-order]]). For $n\in\mathbb Z$, define $|n|=n$ if $0\le n$ and $|n|=-n$ if $n<0$, using the integer order and additive inverse of [[def-int-order]] and [[def-int-operations]]. Totality and compatibility of the integer order with addition ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]) give $0\le|n|$ and $-|n|\le n\le|n|$. Adding these bounds for $m,n\in\mathbb Z$ gives $|m+n|\le|m|+|n|$. Equip $\Gamma$ with the max-coordinate metric $d_\infty(x,y)=\max_{1\le r\le d}|x_r-y_r|$; the maximum exists because the coordinate set is finite and nonempty, symmetry and separation hold coordinatewise, and the absolute-value triangle inequality gives $|x_r-z_r|\le|x_r-y_r|+|y_r-z_r|$ for every coordinate, hence the triangle inequality for $d_\infty$. A **finite region** is a finite subset $\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma$; its cardinality is $|\Lambda|$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]).

For a finite region $\Lambda$, let $S_\Lambda=\{1,\ldots,q\}^{\Lambda}$ be the set of spin configurations on $\Lambda$. Induction on $|\Lambda|$ gives $|S_\Lambda|=q^{|\Lambda|}$: the empty region has one configuration, and adjoining one site multiplies the number of configurations by $q$, according to the recursion defining natural-number powers in [[def-nat-power]]. Let $\mathcal H_\Lambda$ be the vector space of functions $f:S_\Lambda\to\mathbb C$ with inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}f(s)\overline{g(s)}$. For each $s\in S_\Lambda$, let $e_s$ be the indicator function of $\{s\}$; these vectors form an orthonormal basis. For $\Lambda=\varnothing$, $S_\Lambda$ is a singleton and $\mathcal H_\Lambda\cong\mathbb C$. The **local spin matrix algebra** is

$$\mathcal A_\Lambda:=\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)\cong M_{q^{|\Lambda|}}(\mathbb C),$$

Here $\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)$ denotes all complex-linear endomorphisms of the finite-dimensional Hilbert space; they are bounded. The algebra has composition, Hilbert adjoint, identity $I_\Lambda$, and induced operator norm

$$\|T\|:=\sup_{\|\xi\|=1}\|T\xi\|.$$

The **finite local trace** is $\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(T):=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}\langle T e_s,e_s\rangle$ in the displayed configuration basis $(e_s)$. This is the usual finite-matrix trace; basis independence and its cyclic/unitary identities are supplied by [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]].

If $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$, restriction of configurations gives the canonical factorization $\mathcal H_{\Lambda'}\cong\mathcal H_\Lambda\otimes\mathcal H_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$, with sites ordered lexicographically. The **factor inclusion** is the unital $*$-homomorphism $\iota_{\Lambda,\Lambda'}:\mathcal A_\Lambda\to\mathcal A_{\Lambda'}$ given by $T\mapsto T\otimes I_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$. A **localization region** for $T$ is any finite $\Lambda$ for which $T\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ under these inclusions; a localization region need not be minimal.

The ordinary operator norm makes each local matrix algebra a nonzero unital complete C*-algebra, and every positive normalized complex-linear functional is uniquely a trace pairing with a density matrix, by [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]]. This includes the empty region, whose Hilbert space is $\mathbb C$. This definition does not posit an infinite-dimensional tensor-product Hilbert space.

derivations.claim:
For $t=0$, both sides of the stated estimate vanish. For $t\ne0$, put $\sigma=\operatorname{sign}(t)\in\{-1,1\}$, and for $s$ between $0$ and $t$, set $G(s)=\alpha_s^{\Lambda'}(\alpha_{t-s}^{\Lambda}(A))$. Differentiating the finite matrix exponentials gives
$$G'(s)=\frac{i}{\hbar}\alpha_s^{\Lambda'}\!\left([H_{\Lambda'}-H_\Lambda,\alpha_{t-s}^{\Lambda}(A)]\right).$$
Indeed, the derivative of $\alpha_s^{\Lambda'}$ contributes $(i/\hbar)[H_{\Lambda'},\cdot]$, while differentiating $\alpha_{t-s}^{\Lambda}$ contributes $-(i/\hbar)[H_\Lambda,\cdot]$; the outer map $\alpha_s^{\Lambda'}$ is unitary conjugation and hence isometric. Integrating from $0$ to $t$, reversing the orientation for $t<0$, and using $u=|t-s|$ gives intermediate evolution time $t-s=\sigma u$. Expanding $H_{\Lambda'}-H_\Lambda$ therefore yields
$$\|\alpha_t^{\Lambda'}(A)-\alpha_t^\Lambda(A)\|\le\frac1{\hbar}\int_0^{|t|}\sum_{\substack{Z\subseteq\Lambda'\\Z\not\subseteq\Lambda}}\|[\Phi(Z),\alpha_{\sigma u}^\Lambda(A)]\|\,du.$$
Terms with $Z\cap\Lambda=\varnothing$ commute with $\alpha_{\sigma u}^\Lambda(A)\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ and contribute zero; only interaction sets crossing the boundary of $\Lambda$ remain.

For each crossing $Z$, apply [F2] to $A$ and $\Phi(Z)$ at the signed time $\sigma u$. Its bound depends on $|\sigma u|=u$, so the same positive integrand estimate holds for either sign of $t$. For any $y\in Z\setminus\Lambda$, choose $z\in Z$ minimizing the distance from $X$ to $Z$. Since $\operatorname{diam}_\infty Z\le R$, the triangle inequality gives $\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,\{y\})\le\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,Z)+R$, so
$$e^{-\mu\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,Z)}\le e^{\mu R}e^{-\mu\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,\{y\})}.$$
Summing over every exterior $y$ overcounts each crossing interaction and therefore gives an upper bound. By the definition of $\kappa$,
$$\sum_{\substack{Z\subseteq\Lambda'\\Z\not\subseteq\Lambda\\Z\cap\Lambda\ne\varnothing}}\|\Phi(Z)\|e^{-\mu\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,Z)}\le\kappa e^{\mu R}\sum_{y\notin\Lambda}e^{-\mu\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,\{y\})}.$$
The displayed inequality is independent of $\Lambda'$; integrating the time factor in [F2] over an interval of length $|t|$ proves the claimed estimate.

For each $r\ge1$, the max-metric shell around one lattice site has $(2r+1)^d-(2r-1)^d$ sites. A finite union bound over $x\in X$ shows that $\sum_{y\in\mathbb Z^d}e^{-\mu\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,\{y\})}<\infty$, since a polynomial shell count is summable against $e^{-\mu r}$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose a finite set of sites whose omitted tail is below $\varepsilon$; every sufficiently large exhausting $\Lambda$ contains that finite set. Thus the exterior tail tends to zero, uniformly for $|t|\le T$ after replacing $|t|$ by $T$ in the prefactor.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement requires X nonempty, but the exterior aggregate is real: Proof 3.1 proves its convergence and tail vanishing. If there are no crossing interaction terms, the finite sum in 1.1 is0 and the dynamics difference is0.
Steps 1.1 and 2.1: if kappa=0, no boundary interaction contributes and both finite-volume evolutions agree on the local observable.
Step 3.1: for d=1 the max-metric shell has two sites at every positive radius, so the exponential tail is summable.
Steps 1.1–2.1: for R=0 only onsite terms occur, and a crossing term disjoint from the inner volume commutes with its local dynamics.
Step 1.1: t=0 gives zero difference; both signs of t are covered by reversing the integration endpoints and using |t|.
Step 2.1 sums over every exterior site, so it does not choose one site from each crossing interaction.

boundaries.reason: The nested-volume norm estimate implies compact-time Cauchy convergence as the exterior tail vanishes; the claim is not an equivalence with a tail condition.
The estimate in 2.1 is a sufficient bound derived from the interaction norm sum; convergence is not claimed to force that particular bound.

risk_review.notes: Read all steps 1.1–3.1 and all three cited suppliers, after reviewing the path bound. Differentiation gives i/hbar times the Hamiltonian difference. Exterior-disjoint terms commute; summing all exterior incidences overcounts crossing supports, and dist(X,y)<=dist(X,Z)+R gives the e^(mu R) factor and kappa tail. Polynomial lattice shells prove summability; eventual inclusion of a finite tail truncation proves convergence for every exhaustion uniformly on compact times. Checked negative t, t=0, equal volumes, kappa=0, R=0 and q=1. Nachtergaele–Sims Theorem 3.1 equations 3.10–3.16 checked for the comparison method; constants are derived locally. No defect found.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, $D=\dim H\ge1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. With composition, Hilbert adjoint, identity and the induced operator norm, $\mathcal B(H)$ is a nonzero unital complex C*-algebra in the sense of [[def-c-star-algebra]]. In particular it is complete, $\|AB\|\le\|A\|\|B\|$, $\|A^*A\|=\|A\|^2$, $\|A^*\|=\|A\|$ and $\|I\|=1$. The matrix $\|A\|^2I-A^*A$ is positive semidefinite and has a positive square root in $\mathcal B(H)$.

Every complex-linear functional $\omega:\mathcal B(H)\to\mathbb C$ that is positive, meaning $\omega(B^*B)\ge0$ for all $B$, has a unique positive semidefinite matrix $\rho$ such that $\omega(A)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)$ for all $A$. It is bounded and satisfies

$$|\omega(A)|\le\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)\|A\|\quad(A\in\mathcal B(H)),\qquad \|\omega\|=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)=\omega(I).$$

Consequently the canonical states of [[def-state-on-a-c-star-algebra]] are exactly the trace pairings of density operators of [[def-qc-density-operator]]; for a positive functional, normalization $\omega(I)=1$ is equivalent to norm one. The result includes zero positive functionals, nonfaithful densities and $D=1$; it makes no infinite-dimensional density representation assertion.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Cauchy-sequence completion. For the local spin system of [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]], the normed $*$-algebra $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and its completion $\mathcal A$ of [[def-qsm-quasilocal-spin-algebra]] are well defined; $\mathcal A$ is a unital complex C*-algebra and $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is norm dense in it. If $A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ and $B\in\mathcal A_\Delta$ for disjoint finite regions $\Lambda,\Delta$, then $AB=BA$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

$$\mathcal A:=\overline{\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}}^{\,\|\cdot\|}.$$

The C*-algebra structure on this completion has product and adjoint extended continuously from the finite local matrix algebras. Countable Choice is assumed for the published existence theorem for metric completions; [[lem-qsm-quasilocal-completion]] supplies the full extension argument using the finite C*-identity of [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]].

**No global Hilbert tensor product is selected.** “Quasi-local” means norm completion of the directed algebra of finite-region observables; it does not mean a chosen representation as operators on an infinite tensor-product Hilbert space. A local operator $A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ may have more than one localization region. Disjoint finite local factors commute in their common finite tensor algebra.

derivations.claim: Fix local $A\in\mathcal A_X$; if its displayed localization is empty, embed the scalar $A\in\mathbb C I$ into any one-site algebra, so take $X\ne\varnothing$. Let $C_n=\{x\in\mathbb Z^d:d_\infty(x,0)\le n\}$. For all sufficiently large $n$, $C_n\supseteq X$, and for $m\ge n$ the boundary estimate [F3] bounds $\|\alpha_t^{C_m}(A)-\alpha_t^{C_n}(A)\|$ by its right side with $\Lambda=C_n$. That exterior exponential tail tends to zero as $n\to\infty$, uniformly for $|t|\le T$ because its time factor is bounded there. Hence $\alpha_t^{C_n}(A)$ is Cauchy uniformly on compact time intervals; completeness in [A1], [A2], [F1], and [F2] gives a limit $\alpha_t(A)\in\mathcal A$. Given any other increasing finite exhaustion $\Lambda_j$, choose $n$ so large that both the canonical limit error and the [F3] bound for $C_n$ are below $\varepsilon/2$. Since $C_n$ is finite and $\Lambda_j\uparrow\mathbb Z^d$, eventually $C_n\subseteq\Lambda_j$; applying [F3] to this nested pair proves $\alpha_t^{\Lambda_j}(A)\to\alpha_t(A)$ uniformly on $[-T,T]$. Thus the limit is independent of the exhaustion. The finite-matrix premise [A1] is supplied by [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]]; this proof uses that earlier result rather than reproving it.

Every finite-volume map is an isometric unital $*$-automorphism by conjugation with the unitary matrix exponential in [F4]. Norm limits of these complex-linear maps preserve addition and scalar multiplication, so the limit on local observables is complex-linear. The limits also preserve the unit, adjoints, products on local observables, and norm. For products, if local sequences $A_n\to A$ and $B_n\to B$ are used, submultiplicativity gives $\|A_nB_n-AB\|\le\|A_n\|\|B_n-B\|+\|A_n-A\|\|B\|$, so multiplication passes continuously to the completion; the adjoint is norm-continuous as well. By density of $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and the isometry bound, each $\alpha_t$ extends uniquely to an isometric complex-linear unital $*$-homomorphism of $\mathcal A$.

For local $A$, $\alpha_0(A)=\lim_\Lambda\alpha_0^\Lambda(A)=A$, and density extends $\alpha_0=\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal A}$ to all $A\in\mathcal A$. For local $A$ and fixed $s,t$, choose local $C$ with $\|C-\alpha_t(A)\|<\varepsilon$. For large $\Lambda$, both $\alpha_t^\Lambda(A)$ is within $\varepsilon$ of $\alpha_t(A)$ and $\alpha_s^\Lambda(C)$ is within $\varepsilon$ of $\alpha_s(C)$. By isometry, replacing $\alpha_t^\Lambda(A)$ with $C$ in $\alpha_s^\Lambda\alpha_t^\Lambda(A)$ costs at most $2\varepsilon$, and replacing $\alpha_s^\Lambda(C)$ by $\alpha_s(C)$ costs at most $\varepsilon$. The finite-volume group law $\alpha_s^\Lambda\alpha_t^\Lambda(A)=\alpha_{s+t}^\Lambda(A)$ therefore gives $\|\alpha_s\alpha_t(A)-\alpha_{s+t}(A)\|\le4\varepsilon$ after taking limits. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves the group law on local $A$; density extends it to every $A\in\mathcal A$. In particular, $\alpha_{-t}$ is the inverse of $\alpha_t$, so each is bijective and hence an automorphism.

If $A\in\mathcal A_X$ is local, finite-volume differentiation gives
$$\|\alpha_t^\Lambda(A)-A\|\le\frac{|t|}{\hbar}\|[H_\Lambda,A]\|\le\frac{2\kappa |X|\|A\|}{\hbar}|t|,$$
because only terms meeting $X$ contribute and $\sum_{Z\cap X\ne\varnothing}\|\Phi(Z)\|\le\kappa|X|$. Passing to the limit gives continuity at $t=0$ for local $A$. For general $A\in\mathcal A$, choose local $C$ close to $A$ and use $\|\alpha_t(A)-A\|\le2\|A-C\|+\|\alpha_t(C)-C\|$. The group law gives continuity at every time.

Assume Countable Choice and the finite-matrix C*-identity condition [A1] below. Let $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}=\bigcup_{\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d,\ |\Lambda|<\infty}\mathcal A_\Lambda$ and let $\mathcal A$ be its norm completion as in [[def-qsm-quasilocal-spin-algebra]]. These assumptions give the conditional unital C*-algebra structure supplied by [[lem-qsm-quasilocal-completion]]. Let $\Phi$ be a uniformly bounded finite-range interaction of [[def-qsm-bounded-finite-range-interaction]].

For any increasing finite exhaustion $(\Lambda_n)_{n\ge1}$ in the convention of [[lem-qsm-boundary-dynamics-cauchy]]—that is, each $\Lambda_n$ is finite, $\Lambda_n\subseteq\Lambda_{n+1}$, and $\bigcup_{n\ge1}\Lambda_n=\mathbb Z^d$—the free-boundary finite-volume maps $\alpha_t^{\Lambda_n}$ converge in norm on every local observable, uniformly for $t$ in compact intervals. Their limit is independent of the exhaustion and extends uniquely to a strongly continuous one-parameter group $\alpha_t$ of maps $\alpha_t:\mathcal A\to\mathcal A$. Here “one-parameter group” means $\alpha_0=\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal A}$ and $\alpha_{s+t}=\alpha_s\circ\alpha_t$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$. Each $\alpha_t$ is a bijective complex-linear unital $*$-homomorphism (a $*$-automorphism), with inverse $\alpha_{-t}$. Strong continuity means $t\mapsto\alpha_t(A)$ is norm-continuous for every fixed $A\in\mathcal A$. This result does not assert that an infinite-volume Hamiltonian is an element of $\mathcal A$ or a bounded operator on a preselected infinite tensor-product Hilbert space.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, $D=\dim H\ge1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. With composition, Hilbert adjoint, identity and the induced operator norm, $\mathcal B(H)$ is a nonzero unital complex C*-algebra in the sense of [[def-c-star-algebra]]. In particular it is complete, $\|AB\|\le\|A\|\|B\|$, $\|A^*A\|=\|A\|^2$, $\|A^*\|=\|A\|$ and $\|I\|=1$. The matrix $\|A\|^2I-A^*A$ is positive semidefinite and has a positive square root in $\mathcal B(H)$.

Every complex-linear functional $\omega:\mathcal B(H)\to\mathbb C$ that is positive, meaning $\omega(B^*B)\ge0$ for all $B$, has a unique positive semidefinite matrix $\rho$ such that $\omega(A)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)$ for all $A$. It is bounded and satisfies

$$|\omega(A)|\le\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)\|A\|\quad(A\in\mathcal B(H)),\qquad \|\omega\|=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)=\omega(I).$$

Consequently the canonical states of [[def-state-on-a-c-star-algebra]] are exactly the trace pairings of density operators of [[def-qc-density-operator]]; for a positive functional, normalization $\omega(I)=1$ is equivalent to norm one. The result includes zero positive functionals, nonfaithful densities and $D=1$; it makes no infinite-dimensional density representation assertion.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Cauchy-sequence completion. For the local spin system of [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]], the normed $*$-algebra $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and its completion $\mathcal A$ of [[def-qsm-quasilocal-spin-algebra]] are well defined; $\mathcal A$ is a unital complex C*-algebra and $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is norm dense in it. If $A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ and $B\in\mathcal A_\Delta$ for disjoint finite regions $\Lambda,\Delta$, then $AB=BA$.

Let $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}=\bigcup_{\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d,\ |\Lambda|<\infty}\mathcal A_\Lambda$ and let $\mathcal A$ be its norm completion as in [[def-qsm-quasilocal-spin-algebra]]. These assumptions give the conditional unital C*-algebra structure supplied by [[lem-qsm-quasilocal-completion]]. Let $\Phi$ be a uniformly bounded finite-range interaction of [[def-qsm-bounded-finite-range-interaction]].

For any increasing finite exhaustion $(\Lambda_n)_{n\ge1}$ in the convention of [[lem-qsm-boundary-dynamics-cauchy]]—that is, each $\Lambda_n$ is finite, $\Lambda_n\subseteq\Lambda_{n+1}$, and $\bigcup_{n\ge1}\Lambda_n=\mathbb Z^d$—the free-boundary finite-volume maps $\alpha_t^{\Lambda_n}$ converge in norm on every local observable, uniformly for $t$ in compact intervals. Their limit is independent of the exhaustion and extends uniquely to a strongly continuous one-parameter group $\alpha_t$ of maps $\alpha_t:\mathcal A\to\mathcal A$. Here “one-parameter group” means $\alpha_0=\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal A}$ and $\alpha_{s+t}=\alpha_s\circ\alpha_t$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$. Each $\alpha_t$ is a bijective complex-linear unital $*$-homomorphism (a $*$-automorphism), with inverse $\alpha_{-t}$. Strong continuity means $t\mapsto\alpha_t(A)$ is norm-continuous for every fixed $A\in\mathcal A$. This result does not assert that an infinite-volume Hamiltonian is an element of $\mathcal A$ or a bounded operator on a preselected infinite tensor-product Hilbert space.

Let $\Phi$ be an interaction of [[def-qsm-bounded-finite-range-interaction]], fix $\mu>0$, and let $X\subseteq\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$ be finite regions with $X\ne\varnothing$. An **increasing finite exhaustion** of $\mathbb Z^d$ means a sequence of finite regions $(\Lambda_n)_{n\ge1}$ such that $\Lambda_n\subseteq\Lambda_{n+1}$ for every $n$ and $\bigcup_{n\ge1}\Lambda_n=\mathbb Z^d$. For every $A\in\mathcal A_X$ and $t\in\mathbb R$,

$$\|\alpha_t^{\Lambda'}(A)-\alpha_t^\Lambda(A)\|\le\frac{2\kappa |X|\|A\||t|}{\hbar}e^{(2\kappa M e^{\mu R}/\hbar)|t|+\mu R}\sum_{y\notin\Lambda}e^{-\mu\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,\{y\})}.$$

The infinite sum is finite. Along every increasing finite exhaustion $(\Lambda_n)$ as defined above, $\sum_{y\notin\Lambda_n}e^{-\mu\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,\{y\})}\to0$, so the estimate gives compact-time norm Cauchy convergence of free-boundary finite-volume dynamics on each local observable.

Use the lattice $\Gamma=\mathbb Z^d$, $d\ge1$, the finite spin dimension $q\ge1$, the local matrix algebras $\mathcal A_\Lambda$, and the max-coordinate metric $d_\infty$ of [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]]. For finite nonempty $Z\subset\Gamma$, write $\operatorname{diam}_\infty Z=\max_{x,y\in Z}d_\infty(x,y)$; for finite nonempty $X,Y\subset\Gamma$, write $\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,Y)=\min_{x\in X,y\in Y}d_\infty(x,y)$.

A **uniformly bounded finite-range interaction** is a family $\Phi(Z)\in\mathcal A_Z$, indexed by finite nonempty $Z\subset\Gamma$, such that $\Phi(Z)^*=\Phi(Z)$ and there are an integer $M\ge1$, a finite $R\ge0$, and $\kappa<\infty$ satisfying

$$\Phi(Z)=0\quad\text{if }|Z|>M\text{ or }\operatorname{diam}_\infty Z>R,\qquad\kappa:=\sup_{x\in\Gamma}\sum_{Z\ni x}\|\Phi(Z)\|<\infty.$$

The norm in this sum is the operator norm in the local matrix algebra $\mathcal A_Z$. If a model lists several terms with the same support, first add them in that local algebra; the resulting single operator is $\Phi(Z)$, and $\kappa$ uses its norm. Thus no multiplicity is implicit.

For a finite region $\Lambda\subset\Gamma$, define the **free-boundary finite-volume Hamiltonian** by summing only terms whose complete support lies inside $\Lambda$; terms meeting $\Lambda$ but extending outside it are omitted:

$$H_\Lambda:=\sum_{\varnothing\ne Z\subseteq\Lambda}\Phi(Z)\in\mathcal A_\Lambda.$$

It is a finite sum of self-adjoint matrices. For a fixed scale $\hbar>0$ and any finite $\Omega\supseteq\Lambda$, embed $H_\Lambda$ in $\mathcal A_\Omega$ by the canonical factor inclusion and define

$$\alpha_t^\Lambda(A):=e^{itH_\Lambda/\hbar}Ae^{-itH_\Lambda/\hbar}\qquad(A\in\mathcal A_\Omega,\ t\in\mathbb R).$$

These actions are compatible as $\Omega$ increases, because the extra tensor factors carry the identity. On $\mathcal A_\Lambda$ this is the ordinary finite matrix Heisenberg dynamics.

In physical SI bookkeeping, when $\Phi(Z)$ is interpreted as an energy, $\Phi(Z)$, $\kappa$, and $H_\Lambda$ have units J, $t$ has units s, and $\hbar$ is the adopted reduced Planck constant with units J s. The mathematics below uses only $\hbar>0$ and asserts no measured parameter value.

Fix an integer dimension $d\ge1$, the countable site set $\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}^d$ of [[lem-qsm-integer-lattice-countable]], and one finite spin dimension $q\ge1$, where $q$ is a positive integer (so $q\in\mathbb N$ and $1\le q$, by [[def-natural-numbers]] and [[def-nat-order]]). For $n\in\mathbb Z$, define $|n|=n$ if $0\le n$ and $|n|=-n$ if $n<0$, using the integer order and additive inverse of [[def-int-order]] and [[def-int-operations]]. Totality and compatibility of the integer order with addition ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]) give $0\le|n|$ and $-|n|\le n\le|n|$. Adding these bounds for $m,n\in\mathbb Z$ gives $|m+n|\le|m|+|n|$. Equip $\Gamma$ with the max-coordinate metric $d_\infty(x,y)=\max_{1\le r\le d}|x_r-y_r|$; the maximum exists because the coordinate set is finite and nonempty, symmetry and separation hold coordinatewise, and the absolute-value triangle inequality gives $|x_r-z_r|\le|x_r-y_r|+|y_r-z_r|$ for every coordinate, hence the triangle inequality for $d_\infty$. A **finite region** is a finite subset $\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma$; its cardinality is $|\Lambda|$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]).

For a finite region $\Lambda$, let $S_\Lambda=\{1,\ldots,q\}^{\Lambda}$ be the set of spin configurations on $\Lambda$. Induction on $|\Lambda|$ gives $|S_\Lambda|=q^{|\Lambda|}$: the empty region has one configuration, and adjoining one site multiplies the number of configurations by $q$, according to the recursion defining natural-number powers in [[def-nat-power]]. Let $\mathcal H_\Lambda$ be the vector space of functions $f:S_\Lambda\to\mathbb C$ with inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}f(s)\overline{g(s)}$. For each $s\in S_\Lambda$, let $e_s$ be the indicator function of $\{s\}$; these vectors form an orthonormal basis. For $\Lambda=\varnothing$, $S_\Lambda$ is a singleton and $\mathcal H_\Lambda\cong\mathbb C$. The **local spin matrix algebra** is

$$\mathcal A_\Lambda:=\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)\cong M_{q^{|\Lambda|}}(\mathbb C),$$

Here $\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)$ denotes all complex-linear endomorphisms of the finite-dimensional Hilbert space; they are bounded. The algebra has composition, Hilbert adjoint, identity $I_\Lambda$, and induced operator norm

$$\|T\|:=\sup_{\|\xi\|=1}\|T\xi\|.$$

The **finite local trace** is $\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(T):=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}\langle T e_s,e_s\rangle$ in the displayed configuration basis $(e_s)$. This is the usual finite-matrix trace; basis independence and its cyclic/unitary identities are supplied by [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]].

If $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$, restriction of configurations gives the canonical factorization $\mathcal H_{\Lambda'}\cong\mathcal H_\Lambda\otimes\mathcal H_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$, with sites ordered lexicographically. The **factor inclusion** is the unital $*$-homomorphism $\iota_{\Lambda,\Lambda'}:\mathcal A_\Lambda\to\mathcal A_{\Lambda'}$ given by $T\mapsto T\otimes I_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$. A **localization region** for $T$ is any finite $\Lambda$ for which $T\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ under these inclusions; a localization region need not be minimal.

The ordinary operator norm makes each local matrix algebra a nonzero unital complete C*-algebra, and every positive normalized complex-linear functional is uniquely a trace pairing with a density matrix, by [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]]. This includes the empty region, whose Hilbert space is $\mathbb C$. This definition does not posit an infinite-dimensional tensor-product Hilbert space.

derivations.claim:
Every nonzero term $\Phi(Z)$ meeting $X$ has $Z\subseteq X^{+R}:=\{y\in\mathbb Z^d:\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,\{y\})\le R\}$, a finite set. There are finitely many subsets of $X^{+R}$, so
$$D_0(A):=\frac{i}{\hbar}\sum_{Z:\,Z\cap X\ne\varnothing}[\Phi(Z),A]$$
is a finite local sum. If $X\subseteq X'$, each term present in the sum for $X'$ but not for $X$ has support disjoint from $X$ and therefore commutes with $A\in\mathcal A_X$; hence both sums agree. For any two localization regions, compare each with their union to obtain the same conclusion. Thus $D_0(A)$ is independent of the chosen region. For every finite $\Lambda$ containing $X^{+R}$, finite-volume differentiation gives $\delta_\Lambda(A)=\frac{i}{\hbar}[H_\Lambda,A]=D_0(A)$ and
$$\alpha_t^\Lambda(A)-A=\int_0^t\alpha_s^\Lambda(D_0(A))\,ds.$$
Here the finite-dimensional integral is the coordinatewise Riemann integral; differentiating the finite exponential gives the integrand.

By [F2], $\alpha_s^\Lambda(A)$ and $\alpha_s^\Lambda(D_0(A))$ converge in norm uniformly on compact time intervals as $\Lambda$ exhausts the lattice. A continuous Banach-valued function has a Riemann integral because uniform continuity makes its Riemann sums Cauchy in the complete algebra; uniform convergence of the finite-volume integrands lets their integrals pass to the limit. This gives
$$\alpha_t(A)-A=\int_0^t\alpha_s(D_0(A))\,ds.$$
By [F1], $s\mapsto\alpha_s(D_0(A))$ is norm-continuous at $0$; the difference between its average over $[0,t]$ and its value at $0$ is at most $\sup_{|s|\le|t|}\|\alpha_s(D_0(A))-D_0(A)\|$, which tends to zero. Therefore $A\in D(\delta)$ and $\delta(A)=D_0(A)$.

Let $A_n\in D(\delta)$ with $A_n\to A$ and $\delta(A_n)\to B$ in norm. For $h=t/N$, the group law gives the exact telescope
$$\alpha_t(A_n)-A_n=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\alpha_{kh}(\alpha_h(A_n)-A_n)=h\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\alpha_{kh}(\delta(A_n))+h\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\alpha_{kh}\!\left(\frac{\alpha_h(A_n)-A_n}{h}-\delta(A_n)\right).$$
As $N\to\infty$, the second sum has norm at most $|t|\|(\alpha_h(A_n)-A_n)/h-\delta(A_n)\|$, which tends to zero by the definition of $\delta(A_n)$. The first sum is a Riemann sum for the continuous function $s\mapsto\alpha_s(\delta(A_n))$; its integral exists because the algebra is complete and the function is uniformly continuous on compact intervals. Hence $\alpha_t(A_n)-A_n=\int_0^t\alpha_s(\delta(A_n))\,ds$. Isometry bounds the integral of $\alpha_s(\delta(A_n)-B)$ by $|t|\|\delta(A_n)-B\|$, allowing the identity to pass to $\alpha_t(A)-A=\int_0^t\alpha_s(B)\,ds$. Strong continuity bounds the difference between the quotient of this integral and $B$ by $\sup_{|s|\le|t|}\|\alpha_s(B)-B\|$, which tends to zero. Thus $A\in D(\delta)$ and $\delta(A)=B$, proving that the graph of $\delta$ is closed.
